Base directory for this skill: /private/tmp/s1-trig-b/.claude/skills/grilling

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.


ARGUMENTS: Claims status idea — user keeps jumping to solutions, wants assumptions about the problem pulled out first

content.text:
No repo context to lean on — this is all in your head, so I'll pull it out question by question.

One ground rule for your answers: describe **what happens today**, not what should be built. If an answer contains a noun like "dashboard," "portal," or "notification," it's a solution and I'll push back on it.

Round 1 — the root of the tree. Nothing here depends on anything else.

❓ **Q1** — **What kind of claims, and who are the two parties?**: "Claims" could be insurance, warranty/RMA, healthcare billing, expense reimbursement, or a support/dispute process. Name the domain, and name the two sides of a single claim: who files it, and who decides it.

➡️ My guess: insurance-style — an external claimant files, an internal adjuster/reviewer decides, and there's a third party in the middle (broker, repair shop, provider) who neither files nor decides but needs to know. If that third party exists, say so, because it usually turns out to be the one actually generating the pain.

---

❓ **Q2** — **What was the specific incident that made this an idea?**: Not the general theme — the actual moment. A call you took, a complaint someone escalated, a number that looked wrong, a thing you personally had to do by hand at 6pm. Give me one concrete instance with the details intact.

➡️ My guess: someone had to answer "where is my claim?" by manually digging through a system and reading a state back to a person, and it wasn't the first time that week. If you can't produce a specific incident, that itself is the finding — the idea may be a tidiness impulse rather than a felt problem.

---

❓ **Q3** — **Visibility or throughput?**: These are different problems and the whole tree hangs off which one it is. **(a) Visibility:** the claim is moving at an acceptable pace, but the people involved can't see where it is, so they chase. **(b) Throughput:** the claim is genuinely stuck or slow, and "status" is just the symptom you happen to be able to observe. **(c) Both, and you haven't separated them yet.**

➡️ I'd bet (c), and I'd bet the true weight is on (b). Status complaints are the loudest signal of a slow process, and building visibility onto a slow process usually means people now watch, in real time, a thing that still isn't moving. Tell me which, and tell me what evidence you have rather than what you believe.

---

❓ **Q4** — **Does the status actually exist right now?**: If I sat down with your systems today and someone gave me a claim reference, could I determine its true current state? **(a) Yes, it's in one system, someone just has to look.** **(b) Yes, but it's spread across systems/inboxes and has to be assembled by a human.** **(c) No — the real state lives in someone's head or a conversation, and no system knows it.**

➡️ My guess: (c) for the states that matter most. Most claims processes have clean recorded states for the boring transitions and no recorded state at all for "waiting on the customer to send a photo" or "flagged to a senior for a second opinion" — which are precisely the states people call about. If it's (c), a status feature is a data-capture problem wearing a display problem's clothing.

---

❓ **Q5** — **What do people do today instead, and what does that cost?**: There's an existing workaround, because there always is. Who does it, how often, how long does it take, and what happens if they don't do it? Rough numbers are fine, but I want the units — calls per day, minutes per call, claims per adjuster.

➡️ My guess: inbound calls and emails asking "any update?", absorbed by whoever answers the phone, unmeasured, and nobody has ever counted them. If nobody has counted, say "nobody has counted" — I'd rather have an admitted gap than an invented number.

Answer all five and I'll recompute the frontier.
